newsitem.title: CANADA: Large Prairie crop a blessing, burden - CWB's Hehn.
newsitem.headline: Large Prairie crop a blessing, burden - CWB's Hehn.

text.p: A large Prairie crop this year should help Canadian exporters gain wider market share but could create and fall prey to transportation bottlenecks, the Canadian Wheat Board's chief commissioner told Reuters.
"It's going to be a real challenge to move this crop to market. The challenge is going to be to ensure nothing happens in the transportation and handling," CWB's Lorne Hehn said in an interview.
Hehn estimated Prairie wheat, barley, canola, oats, flax and rye output in crop year 1996/97 (Aug/July) at 52 million to 53 million tonnes, up 12.5 percent from 46.2 million last year.
Canada's primary and terminal grain elevators turn their stocks over more often than U.S. facilities, relying on just-in-time delivery.
Grain and oilseed exports were hamstrung early in 1994 and again in 1995 by port and railway strikes.
Shipments were backed up for weeks after the strikes ended as bottle necks developed throughout the handling system.

"This additional volume means we'll be able to service some of those markets in the Far East and Latin America that require a higher quality protein grain that we haven't be able to service to the extent we'd like," Hehn said.
Taiwan, for example, demands 14.0 percent protein content on the milling wheat it buys, he said.
Taiwan, Malaysia and South Korea may buy more CWB grains because of better quality prospects this year, Hehn said.

Asked whether the CWB would maintain its traditional 50 percent share of China's wheat imports despite better Chinese output and cancellation of U.S. wheat contracts, Hehn said: "China doesn't always import according to their crop. They look at price and they look at quality and their needs for blending. They're getting more food-safety conscious all the time, like other countries."
Canada exported 4.79 million tonnes of wheat, excluding durum, to China in 1995/96 (Aug/July), down from 5.17 million tonnes in 1994/95, Canadian Grain Commission figures show.
Japan, the CWB's second largest customer requires more than 35 chemical residue tests on every cargo, he added.
"We use very little insecticide in post-harvest because of the cold winter we have," Hehn said.

Japan bought 1.36 million tonnes of wheat from Canada in the last crop year, up from 1.34 million the year before. Brazil was the third largest importer at 1.1 million tonnes and Indonesia was fourth at 899,000 tonnes, CGC figures show.
